> You have labels. You want to extend them to new cases. This is the most
> common — and most over-applied — setup in biology.

## Learning objectives

1. Fit and interpret a logistic regression.
2. Read a confusion matrix.
3. Explain why interpretable coefficients often beat a small accuracy gain.
4. Recognise when your labels, not your model, are the problem.

## Start with regression

Logistic regression is a machine learning model. It is also interpretable,
fast, and hard to overfit with few predictors. In clinical genomics that
combination is difficult to beat.

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit <- glm(outcome ~ predictor1 + predictor2,
           data = train, family = binomial)
summary(fit)
exp(coef(fit))   # odds ratios
```

An odds ratio is something you can put in a paper and defend to a clinician.

## The confusion matrix

|  | Predicted + | Predicted − |
|---|---|---|
| **Actually +** | True positive | False negative |
| **Actually −** | False positive | True negative |

Everything — sensitivity, specificity, precision — comes from these four
numbers. Report the matrix, not just a summary statistic derived from it.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two errors are not equal
Missing a treatable infection is not the same as an unnecessary follow-up test.
Your metric must reflect which error is worse *in your setting*. No default does
this for you.
:::

## How many predictors can I afford?

Roughly **10 events per predictor**. With 40 cases you can justify about four
variables. This constraint is not negotiable by using a fancier model — a
flexible model with 40 events overfits harder, not less.

## When labels are the problem

Your model inherits every bias in its labels. If severe cases were
preferentially tested, "predicts disease" may really mean "predicts who got
tested".

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ask how labels were assigned
Before training: who decided, using what criteria, on which patients? If labels
came from a biased process, high accuracy means you reproduced the bias
faithfully.
:::

## Exercises

1. Fit a logistic regression and interpret the odds ratios in plain language.
2. Build the confusion matrix at thresholds 0.3, 0.5, 0.7. What moves?
3. Given 40 events, how many predictors are defensible? What happens at 20?

## Takeaways

- Regression first; justify anything more complex.
- Report the confusion matrix.
- Interrogate your labels before your model.
